title: Demand and Supply of Infrequent Payments as a Commitment Device: Evidence from Kenya
research_question: Do producers value receiving lump-sum, infrequent payments for frequently provided goods, and are they willing to incur sizable costs to obtain them as a way to commit to saving for lumpy expenses? On the supply side, what determines which buyers are able to offer such infrequent payments, and in particular, does limited contractual credibility of buyers restrict competition in providing this commitment service?
data_description: The study combines original survey data and multiple experiments conducted in the Kenyan dairy sector in Kiambu County, Central Kenya, during 2014 and 2017. A baseline survey covers approximately 596 dairy farmers selling to a large cooperative and to itinerant traders, capturing saving goals, payment preferences, trust in buyers, household demographics, herd size, and milk production. Two field experiments with coop members (around 96 and 95 farmers) elicit choices over daily versus monthly payment schedules at varying prices. Lab-in-the-field experiments include 191 farmers eliciting reservation prices for monthly versus daily payments and 55 farmer-trader pairs testing buyer credibility. A field experiment with 398 farmers tests sale responses to price and payment-flexibility variation. Additional surveys cover Kenyan tea growers (100), Myanmar garment supervisors (34), and Rwandan coffee mills (198). The unit of observation is the farmer, transaction, or firm, depending on the design.
institutional_context: Dairy is the largest agricultural sector in Kenya, dominated by smallholders owning one to three cows who milk twice daily and sell perishable milk through twice-daily transactions. In Kiambu County, two buyer types coexist: a large, long-established cooperative with about 2,000 members operating 24 fixed collection centers and paying farmers once a month via direct bank deposit, and numerous small itinerant traders who buy smaller quantities and pay daily, in cash or via mobile money. Traders typically offer roughly 20 percent higher per-liter prices than the cooperative. Farmers face lumpy expenses (school fees, durables, household investments) and have limited access to effective commitment savings products; informal saving groups and bank accounts are common but imperfect. Traders are mobile, with high turnover and limited information sharing across villages, while the cooperative is a visible, geographically anchored institution, generating sharp differences in the credibility of long-horizon payment promises.
